https://www.dw.com/en/germany-more-power.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ii9Z Germany is set to give its intelligence agencies new powers Image: imago/bonn-sequenz Advertisement The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (Bundesverfassungsschutz, BfV) and the Federal Intelligence Service (Bundesnachrichtendienst, BND) are secret services. Both operate covertly — the former domestically, the latter abroad. They have long complained that they have fewer powers than their counterparts in other countries. To better defend Germany against internal and external threats, the cabinet approved a draft bill on Wednesday . Parliamentary approval is still pending; the MPs' summer recess ends in early September. However, it is considered a mere formality that the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, with the government majority of conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) and center-left Social Democrats (SPD), will give it the green light. Germany's largest intelligence reform since World War II A new era for the German intelligence services is then expected to begin in early 2027. Their scope of operations would extend far beyond their current powers. It would then be possible, for example, to counter a cyberattack by neutralizing enemy IT systems. What is cyber warfare? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Should a state of tension or military defense arise, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) could carry out acts of sabotage abroad. In addition, the BND, like the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, would be given the ability to manipulate or delete data. Proponents and opponents alike agree that this reform would be the largest in German history since the end of World War II in 1945. Intelligence services and police: Will they remain separate? After World War II, as a lesson learned from the atrocities committed by the Secret State Police (Gestapo) during the Nazi era, separate areas of responsibility were established in West Germany . Since then, intelligence services have been primarily responsible for gathering information, while the police handle threat prevention and law enforcement. This so-called principle of separation is now in jeopardy. Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) speaks of "real intelligence agencies" and hopes that the planned reform will result in a more stable security architecture. "Sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks and covert operations by foreign powers require new responses," Dobrindt said. The agencies would be granted operational capabilities and active powers to effectively combat modern state terrorism and extremist violence. AI and drones: Possibilities and Risks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Is the draft bill unconstitutional? The BND and the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution are also set to be granted new powers in their traditional core mission of collecting and analyzing information. These include the analysis of large volumes of data using artificial intelligence (AI) and the cross-referencing of biometric data with the internet. Data retention periods are also set to be extended. The Society for Civil Rights (GFF) considers large parts of the federal government's draft bill — which spans more than 700 pages — to be unconstitutional. With regard to the domestic intelligence service, the far-reaching access to private and public video surveillance in real time is seen as particularly problematic, GFF expert Kai Dittmann replied in response to a written inquiry from DW. The donation-funded nonprofit GFF believes the same applies to biometric matching against publicly available images on the internet and the training of AI using data collected by intelligence agencies. "There are no sufficient and clearly defined limits for such far-reaching intrusions, which above all affect countless innocent people," Dittmann criticizes. The GFF argues the planned additional powers for the BND would violate constitutional rights: The foreign intelligence service would no longer be limited to gathering intelligence, but would also be tasked with warding off threats, operating domestically and carrying out active cyber operations. "This blurs the constitutional boundaries between intelligence services, the police and the military," Dittmann says. Germany's spy chief believes US cooperation will continue To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Will there still be parliamentary control? The GFF also has serious concerns regarding the proposed reform of intelligence agency oversight, which is to be consolidated under the Independent Oversight Council. At the same time, there are plans to largely strip the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) of its authority to oversee intelligence activities. Dittmann's conclusion: "The agencies are gaining significantly more power, while oversight is likely to be weakened." Clara Bünger, the domestic policy expert for the opposition socialist Left Party in the Bundestag, echoes this sentiment: "Because the intelligence agencies will no longer be required to inform those affected in many cases, effective legal protection is no longer guaranteed." Bünger announced that the Left Party will oppose what they see as authoritarian restructuring of the state. "There must never again be a secret police in Germany," she said. The Association of the Internet Industry (eco) has also expressed concerns: In light of the changing security landscape, intelligence agencies need modern technical capabilities, emphasizes board member Klaus Landefeld. "But the line is crossed when the state develops an interest in keeping security gaps open so it can continue to have access. Vulnerabilities must be closed and must not become a tool for intelligence agency access," Landefeld added. Meanwhile, Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the Parliamentary Oversight Committee for the Intelligence Services, has no such concerns. "I believe it's time to trust our own government, including our own security agencies," the Christian Democrat said in a Table Media podcast. Germany has the best-regulated intelligence services in the world, he said, and that should remain the case. This article has been translated from German. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Sudan Humanitarian crisis worsening in refuge for civilians fleeing Sudan’s civil war Conditions are deteriorating in city of El Obeid and camps on its outskirts, with more people arriving every day Rachel Savage in Johannesburg Sun 30 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 02.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside. The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children. “The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety. The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.” The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago. View image in fullscreen Tens of thousands of people are living in tented camps around El Obeid. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August. “During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.” Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict . Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine . Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands . More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege. View image in fullscreen The damaged interior of a lawyers' syndicate in El Obeid, reportedly targeted by the RSF in July. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images A surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in June led the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher. The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city. Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.” Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group. Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.” So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers , a non-governmental group. With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year. View image in fullscreen Conditions in the camps around El Obeid are said to be poor. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Meanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June. “The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.” Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.” Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.” Explore more on these topics Sudan Africa Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA UK security and counter-terrorism Rightwing extremists increasingly likely to consider terrorist attacks, MI5 chief says Move from anti-immigration or anti-Muslim views to violence is ‘most marked trend’ in spy agency’s caseload over last year Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Extremists holding anti-immigration opinions are becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels in the UK, the head of MI5 has warned. Ken McCallum said a shift from radicalised rightwing sentiment to violence was “the most marked trend” in the spy agency’s caseload over the past year, contributing to a rise in the overall UK terror threat level. In an annual threat update, the director general said there had been an increase in cases where “extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent”, such as planning attacks on migrants and Muslims. A number of aggressive anti-migrant protests have been held this autumn by the far-right Patriot Platform at Portsmouth and Dover, while racially and religiously motivated offences are running at record levels. From black-clad agitators to an appeal for ‘Tommo’s Mum’: an unsettling week with the Patriot Platform Read more McCallum said young people were particularly likely to gravitate towards extreme rightwing terrorism, and at one point this year the Security Service was “investigating a radicalised … 13-year-old in the UK”. A year ago, he added, a 16-year-old from Inverclyde received a 10-year prison sentence after he pleaded guility to planning mass murder by firebombing a Muslim centre in Greenock. The warning formed part of a wide-ranging update from the spy chief at MI5’s London headquarters near Westminster on Tuesday morning. He said Iran was trying to expand hostile activities in the UK and it now had “ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites”, such as the RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire. In the past year, MI5’s counter-Iran operation had led to more than 50 arrests in the UK, with much of Tehran’s increased aggression aimed at “British Jewish communities” including terrorist plots and arson attacks against synagogues, business and ambulances. McCallum also said that: Russia remains “aggressor number one” as the Kremlin continues to lash out against the west with assassination plots, explosive threats and cyber-attacks that at times stop “not much short” of conventional warfare. Moscow tried to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media, and via troll social media accounts, but there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”. He was “particularly focused” on the risk of hostile states or terrorists using AI to generate new, deadly bioweapons, and announced the creation of a new AI threat assessment centre to distinguish fact from fiction. There was a “concerning trend of violence targeted at political figures, religious or community groups”, as demonstrated by the killing of the former minister and Reform UK spokesperson Anne Widdecombe. Threats from other states had quadrupled in the last decade and were running on par with MI5’s counter-terrorism mission. “We have again entered a new era of national security,” he said.
